'''Yuri Antonievich Izrael''' ({{langx|ru|Юрий Антониевич Израэль}}; 15 May 1930, [[Tashkent]] – 23 January 2014, [[Moscow]]) was a Soviet and Russian meteorologist. He served as the vice-chairman of the [[Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change]] (IPCC) until September 2008, when the new bureau was elected.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.iisd.ca/vol12/enb12384e.html#ELECTIONOFTHEBUREAUANDTHETASKFORCEBUREAU |title=Summary of the 29th session of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change|access-date=2009-12-24|work=[[Earth Negotiations Bulletin]]|publisher=[[International Institute for Sustainable Development|International Institute for Sustainable Development – Reporting Services Division]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.ipcc.ch/meetings/session29/FINAL_REPT_P_29.pdf|title=Report of the 29th session of the IPCC|access-date=2009-12-24|work=Meeting Documentation |publisher=[[Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change]]}}</ref> He was the "most influential scientific adviser" for [[Vladimir Putin]], the president of Russia, according to [[CNN]].<ref name=CNN>{{cite news|url=http://www.cnn.com/2003/ALLPOLITICS/10/16/column.novak.opinion.russian/|title=The Russian didn't bark|access-date=2007-05-25|last=Novak|first=Robert|author-link=Robert Novak|date=2003-10-16|agency=[[CNN]]|archive-date=26 October 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121026104544/http://www.cnn.com/2003/ALLPOLITICS/10/16/column.novak.opinion.russian/|url-status=bot: unknown}}</ref>

Izrael was former chairman of the Committee for [[Hydrometeorology]]. He also served as director of the Institute of Global Climate and Ecology, which is a part of the [[Russian Academy of Sciences]]. He was a first vice-president of the [[World Meteorological Organization]] and helped develop the World Weather Watch.<ref name="UNEP">{{cite web |url=http://staging.unep.org/sasakawa/winners/yuri.asp |title=Professor Yuri Izrael: Co-Winner 1992|access-date=2017-04-03|work=UNEP Sasakawa Environment Prize (1992) |publisher=[[United Nations Environment Programme]]}}</ref>

In 1992, Izrael won the [[International Meteorological Organization Prize]] and the [[United Nations Environment Programme|UNEP]] Sasakawa Environment Prize for, among other accomplishments, contributing to the "success of Working Group I I" of the IPCC.<ref name=UNEP/>

==Views on the Kyoto Protocol==
Since 2001, the Russian president Vladimir Putin had received a large number of appeals from the heads of foreign states about the need for Russia to ratify the Kyoto Protocol. At a meeting of the Security Council, Vladimir Putin instructed his advisor [[Andrey Illarionov]] to find out whether the ratification of the Kyoto Protocol was in Russia's national interest. Not trusting to experts from [[Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change]], Andrey Illarionov decided to address the President of the Russian Academy of Sciences, [[Yury Osipov]], and Yuri Israel, with a request to involve Russian leading scientists in the discussion of this issue. On January 16, 2004, the first meeting of a scientific seminar on the adoption of the Kyoto Protocol took place at the Russian Academy of Sciences, when Yuri Israel headed the seminar. Yuri Izrael proposed to influence the climate by removing carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and introducing an additional amount of aerosols into the stratosphere. He also pointed to the dual role of carbon dioxide: doubling its quantity in the atmosphere made it possible to increase the yields of major crops, but this fact was outweighed by the negative aspects of anthropogenic warming.<ref>{{cite book | chapter-url=https://doi.org/10.21467/abstracts.93.41 | doi=10.21467/abstracts.93.41 | chapter=The Activities of the Russian Academy of Science's Council Concerning the Kyoto Protocol and Discussions Around Climate Change | title=Abstracts of the Second Eurasian RISK-2020 Conference and Symposium | year=2020 | isbn=9788194270942 | s2cid=226007853 }}</ref>

Yuri Izrael believed the [[Kyoto Protocol]], an international treaty aimed at reducing global [[greenhouse gas emissions]], is not scientifically supported and damaging for the Russian economy,<ref>{{cite news|title=Academician Izrael: Kyoto Protocol economically hazardous to Russi|url=http://newsfromrussia.com/world/2004/07/17/55051.html|publisher=[[RIA Novosti]]|date=2004-07-17|access-date=2007-05-25|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070621012400/http://newsfromrussia.com/world/2004/07/17/55051.html|archive-date=2007-06-21|url-status=dead}}</ref> stating, "the Kyoto Protocol is overly expensive, ineffective and based on bad science."<ref name=CNN/><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.cei.org/gencon/003,03694.cfm|title=Global Warming Shakeup in Moscow. Scientific Conference Signals Sea Change in Climate Debate|access-date=2007-05-25|date=2003-10-09|format=[[Adobe ColdFusion|cfm]]|publisher=[[Competitive Enterprise Institute]]|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120415114723/http://cei.org/news-releases/global-warming-shakeup-moscow|archive-date=2012-04-15}}</ref>

==Views on global warming==
Izrael stated, "climate change is obvious, but science has not yet been able to identify the causes of it," and, "there is no proven link between human activity and global warming."{{citation needed|date=November 2020}} This was a statement seemingly made in stark contrast to the [[Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change|IPCC]] conclusion that "most of the observed increase in globally averaged temperatures since the mid-20th century is ''very likely'' [confidence level >90%] due to the observed increase in anthropogenic [human] greenhouse gas concentrations."<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.ipcc.ch/SPM2feb07.pdf|title=Summary for Policymakers|work=Climate Change 2007: The Physical Science Basis. Contribution of Working Group I to the Fourth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change|access-date=2007-02-02|date=2007-02-05|publisher=[[Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change]]|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070203164304/http://www.ipcc.ch/SPM2feb07.pdf|archive-date=2007-02-03|url-status=dead}}</ref>

Izrael agreed with the IPCC predictions for future climate change, stating, "Global temperatures will likely rise by 1.4-5.8 degrees during the next 100 years. The average increase will be three degrees. I do not think that this threatens mankind. Sea levels, due to rise by 47 cm in the 21st century, will not threaten port cities." He also states, "I think the panic over global warming is totally unjustified. There is no serious threat to the climate," and, "There is no need to dramatize the anthropogenic impact, because the climate has always been subject to change under Nature's influence, even when humanity did not even exist."{{citation needed|date=November 2020}} Additionally, he did not believe the 0.6&nbsp;°[[Celsius|C]] (1.08&nbsp;°[[Fahrenheit|F]]) rise in temperature observed in the last 100 years is a threat, stating, "there is no scientifically sound evidence of the negative processes that allegedly begin to take place at such temperatures."{{citation needed|date=November 2020}}

Instead of decreasing [[carbon dioxide]], he argued, aerosol injections in to the stratosphere would be a more effective way to [[Climate change mitigation|mitigate global warming]].{{citation needed|date=November 2020}} He appeared to favor adaption over mitigation, arguing, "The people of Bangladesh, who live at sea level, may face problems if the Indian Ocean rises. Still, their resettlement would be much cheaper than projected Kyoto Protocol expenses."{{citation needed|date=November 2020}}

==Criticism==
Izrael was chairman of the State Committee on Hydrometeorology (''Goskomgidromet'') at the time of the [[Chernobyl disaster|Chernobyl nuclear accident]]. Following the accident he was widely criticized for slow and inaccurate monitoring. He was also criticized for allowing air pollution throughout the Soviet Union to reach unprecedented levels.<ref>{{cite journal|last= Robinson|first=Nicholas A.|date=January 1989|title=Soviet Environmental Protection: The Challenge for Legal Studies|journal=Pace Environmental Law Review|volume=7|pages=117–150|doi=10.58948/0738-6206.1541 |url=http://digitalcommons.pace.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1382&context=lawfaculty|format=PDF|access-date=2008-02-14|url-access=subscription}}</ref> In a 2004 article published in ''[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]'', Quirin Schiermeier and Bryon MacWilliams referred to him as a "fossil communist fighting for fossil fuel."<ref>{{cite journal|last=Schiermeier|first=Quirin|author2= MacWilliams, Bryon|date=2004-09-01|title=Climate change: Crunch time for Kyoto|journal=[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]|volume=431|issue=7004|pages=12–13|doi=10.1038/431012a |pmid=15343303|doi-access=free}}</ref>
